paragraphs: This paper examines how knowledge learned in one domain can help classification in a related domain with few labeled examples. It compares three research directions: transferring trained network weights, learning embeddings that represent class structure, and methods designed specifically for few-shot learning. Bringing these approaches into one comparison helps clarify which parts of transfer are most useful.

The authors also develop hybrid methods that adapt a source-trained embedding using the limited labeled data available in the target domain. This makes the representation itself adjustable to the new task. Their systematic evaluation varies both the number of labeled target examples and the number of target classes across multiple domains.

In these comparisons, deep embeddings provide substantially better starting points than weight transfer. The hybrid methods outperform the evaluated previous few-shot and metric-learning approaches, with a reported mean error reduction of 34%. Histogram loss is the most robust embedding loss in the study. These empirical findings support studying representation learning and target-domain adaptation together.
neurips-2018-adapted-deep-embeddings-a-s.tldr: Adapting source-trained embeddings with limited target data improves few-shot transfer across the paper’s systematic comparisons.

paragraphs: This paper studies streaming principal component analysis when observations arrive as a stationary time series. The target is a principal component of the covariance matrix associated with the stationary distribution. Unlike a setting with independent observations, dependence between successive data points complicates the behavior and analysis of stochastic optimization.

The proposed method combines a variant of Oja’s algorithm with downsampling. Downsampling controls the bias in stochastic gradients caused by dependence in the data. This addresses a specific obstacle to estimating a useful low-dimensional direction while processing a time series incrementally, rather than assuming that each new observation supplies independent information.

The theoretical analysis uses diffusion approximations to quantify uncertainty in the algorithm’s evolution. From this analysis, the authors establish an asymptotic convergence rate and obtain near-optimal asymptotic sample complexity. Numerical experiments support the analysis. The contribution connects an implementable streaming procedure with guarantees for dependent, stationary data, while the stated rate and sample-efficiency conclusions concern asymptotic behavior.
neurips-2018-dimensionality-reduction-fo.tldr: A downsampled variant of Oja’s algorithm provides streaming PCA guarantees for dependent, stationary time-series data.

paragraphs: This paper develops a one-pass algorithm for selecting a valuable feasible subset from a data stream under a submodular objective. Its central idea is to subsample incoming elements so that the algorithm need not evaluate every element even once. This combines limited-memory processing with a reduction in potentially expensive function evaluations.

For a monotone objective under a p-matchoid constraint, the randomized algorithm has a 4p approximation ratio in expectation. It uses O(k) memory and O(km/p) queries per element, where k is the largest feasible solution size and m counts the matroids defining the constraint. For non-monotone objectives, the ratio becomes 4p+2-o(1), preserving a closely related guarantee.

The experiments connect these theoretical savings to practical workloads. On video summarization, the authors report speedups of up to fifty-fold over the compared state-of-the-art algorithm while retaining practically the same utility. They also evaluate scalability using Uber pickup locations. The results show how evaluating fewer stream elements can substantially reduce computation without a comparable observed loss in solution quality.
neurips-2018-do-less-get-more-streaming-.tldr: Careful subsampling reduces streaming submodular optimization costs while retaining strong expected approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to certify that an input cannot be turned into an adversarial example by a sufficiently small change. The goal is a certified lower bound on the minimum distortion needed to alter a neural classifier’s prediction. Such a bound gives a guaranteed region of robustness without requiring the exact minimum distortion to be found.

The authors introduce CROWN, which handles general activation functions by bounding them with linear and quadratic functions. It can work with ReLU, tanh, sigmoid, and arctan, among other choices. The method adaptively selects suitable bounding surrogates for individual neurons to seek tighter certificates, extending certification beyond approaches centered on ReLU’s piecewise-linear structure.

Experiments on ReLU networks show stronger certified lower bounds than Fast-Lin with comparable computational efficiency. Experiments with the other listed activations demonstrate the framework’s flexibility and effectiveness. These findings concern the strength and computational cost of robustness certificates: improving a lower bound means certifying a larger protected region, rather than establishing the exact location of the nearest adversarial example.
neurips-2018-efficient-neural-network-ro.tldr: CROWN certifies robustness across general activation functions using adaptive linear and quadratic bounds.

paragraphs: This paper accelerates a computation used to infer evolutionary trees under the perfect phylogeny model. The observations are mutation frequencies: fractions of genomes carrying mutations at different positions across samples. Finding a suitable tree can require searching a large space of possibilities, making the cost of evaluating each candidate especially important.

At the center of that evaluation is a projection problem that assigns a fitness cost to a candidate tree. The authors develop a new projection algorithm using Moreau’s decomposition for proximal operators together with a tree reduction scheme. The algorithm reaches an exact solution after finitely many steps, providing a precise evaluation procedure for the surrounding tree search.

The reported computational result illustrates why this inner operation matters: the method enables a search over more than two billion evolutionary trees with fewer than 11 nodes in about two hours. That size is relevant to several biological problems described by the authors. The contribution is therefore an exact and fast building block that makes extensive exploration of candidate phylogenies more practical.
neurips-2018-efficient-projection-onto-t.tldr: An exact, finite-step projection algorithm makes extensive searches over small perfect-phylogeny trees practical.

paragraphs: Glow is a generative model built around a flow architecture using invertible 1x1 convolutions. The paper’s motivation is that flow-based models combine several attractive computational properties: exact log-likelihood can be evaluated, latent variables can be inferred exactly, and both training and generation can be parallelized. These properties connect image generation with a tractable probabilistic model.

The proposed architecture uses an invertible convolution as a central component of a comparatively simple generative flow. Invertibility matters because the model retains the ability to move between observed data and its latent representation. The paper therefore focuses on an architectural choice within a family that already supports exact likelihood and latent-variable inference.

The authors report significant improvements in log-likelihood and qualitative sample quality. They also demonstrate efficient generation of large images that look realistic by subjective assessment, despite training with the plain log-likelihood objective. This finding shows that likelihood-focused training can produce visually convincing samples in their setting; the stated visual-quality assessment remains qualitative.
neurips-2018-glow-generative-flow-with-i.tldr: Glow uses invertible 1x1 convolutions to improve flow-based image generation while retaining exact likelihood and latent inference.

paragraphs: Training convolutional networks across multiple workers requires combining their gradients, and communication can consume much of the potential speedup. Existing scalar compression techniques can work poorly with ring all-reduce because their compressed gradients cannot be aggregated directly. This paper treats compatibility with aggregation as a central requirement for useful compression.

The authors empirically identify strong linear correlations among CNN gradients and introduce GradiVeQ to exploit them. It uses principal component analysis to reduce gradient dimensionality through vector quantization. Because the resulting compressed gradients can be aggregated directly, the system can run gradient compression and ring all-reduce communication in parallel.

Experiments on popular CNNs report more than a fivefold reduction in gradient aggregation time relative to the original ring all-reduce, without noticeable accuracy loss. Overall training time falls by almost 50%. GradiVeQ is also compatible with scalar quantization such as QSGD and achieves greater speedup at the same compression ratio. The results highlight that compression’s practical value depends on how well it fits the communication procedure.
neurips-2018-gradiveq-vector-quantizatio.tldr: GradiVeQ compresses correlated CNN gradients into a directly aggregatable representation, substantially reducing distributed training time in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether model-free reinforcement learning can learn efficiently from interactions, even in the basic setting of finitely many states and actions. Model-free methods update values or policies directly rather than constructing an environment model. Their practical popularity makes it important to understand whether their apparent demand for many samples is unavoidable.

The authors analyze Q-learning equipped with upper-confidence-bound exploration in an episodic Markov decision process. They prove a regret bound of approximately sqrt(H³SAT), suppressing logarithmic factors. Here S and A count states and actions, H is the episode length, and T is the total number of interaction steps. The bound is within a factor of sqrt(H) of optimal regret.

This result establishes sample efficiency for the analyzed classical model-free approach. Its square-root dependence on T means cumulative regret grows sublinearly with experience. The analysis does not require a simulator, and the authors identify it as the first model-free square-root-T regret result with that property. The guarantee specifically concerns the stated episodic setting and exploration-equipped Q-learning algorithm.
neurips-2018-is-q-learning-provably-effi.tldr: Q-learning with UCB exploration achieves near-optimal regret in finite episodic environments without requiring a simulator.

paragraphs: KONG develops graph comparison methods for labeled graphs whose neighboring nodes have a meaningful order. Such order arises naturally when edges are added over time: the sequence of edge creation supplies information beyond connectivity and labels. The paper investigates how to preserve that additional structure when building features for graph learning.

The proposed kernels combine convolutional subgraph kernels with string kernels, bringing together methods for graph structure and ordered sequences. Sketching techniques produce explicit feature maps through scalable algorithms. The authors derive precise bounds on approximation accuracy and computational complexity, making both the computational savings and the quality of the approximation part of the analysis.

Experiments on real datasets show that using neighborhood order produces more informative features. This supports treating order as useful data when it is available, rather than discarding it during representation. The framework also covers graphs without ordered neighborhoods. In that special case, the resulting kernels give simple and efficient algorithms for comparing label distributions between graphs.
neurips-2018-kong-kernels-for-ordered-ne.tldr: KONG combines graph and sequence kernels to create scalable features that retain meaningful neighborhood order.

paragraphs: This paper changes the objective used to learn Gaussian process models. Although these models are broadly useful for supervised learning, the authors identify weak performance guarantees as an obstacle to safety-critical use. Their approach makes a bound on generalization performance the quantity optimized during learning, directly connecting training to a theoretical performance guarantee.

The method minimizes a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound rather than maximizing marginal likelihood. It applies both to Gaussian processes and to sparse approximations of them. This is significant because the proposed training principle extends to approximations used when working with larger datasets, rather than being confined to the full model.

On several regression benchmarks, the authors find that the method is robust and provides significantly better generalization guarantees than common Gaussian process approaches. The stated improvement is in the guarantees obtained through evaluation, not a claim that every predictive metric improves in every application. The work shows how a guarantee-oriented objective can serve as a practical learning criterion for probabilistic regression.
neurips-2018-learning-gaussian-processes.tldr: Training Gaussian processes by minimizing PAC-Bayesian bounds yields stronger generalization guarantees on several regression benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a model can learn which changes to an input should leave its prediction unchanged. Such invariances are often imposed through data augmentation, where a person chooses transformations and adds modified examples to the training set. The authors argue for placing invariances within the model structure and learning them through marginal likelihood.

Their reasoning is that marginal likelihood can reward the reduction in model complexity that comes from invariance. They use Gaussian processes because suitable approximations to marginal likelihood are available for this model family. This connects the choice of invariance to a probabilistic learning criterion instead of treating the transformation rule only as an external training-data choice.

The main contribution is a variational inference scheme for invariant Gaussian processes. It handles invariance described through a probability distribution from which samples can be drawn, resembling the sampling mechanism used in practical data augmentation. The resulting formulation brings a familiar way of specifying transformations into structured probabilistic inference, making invariance part of the model being learned.
neurips-2018-learning-invariances-using-.tldr: A variational inference scheme incorporates sampled invariances into Gaussian processes and supports learning them through marginal likelihood.

paragraphs: NEON2 addresses nonconvex optimization, where finding a stationary point does not by itself establish that the point is a local minimum. The paper proposes a reduction that upgrades stationary-point methods into local-minimum methods. This makes the contribution reusable across optimization algorithms, rather than tying it to one particular update rule.

The reduction also replaces Hessian-vector product calculations with gradient calculations alone. Hessian-vector products provide second-order information, while gradients are first-order information. The authors state that this replacement works in both stochastic and deterministic settings without degrading the algorithm’s performance. Thus, the approach connects a stronger optimization target with a simpler information requirement.

As one application, the reduction makes Natasha2 a first-order method while preserving its theoretical performance. It also converts SGD, GD, SCSG, and SVRG into methods for finding approximate local minima, improving on some previously best-known results. These applications show the reduction’s breadth. The local-minimum conclusions concern approximate local solutions and do not assert that the methods find globally optimal solutions.
neurips-2018-neon2-finding-local-minima-.tldr: NEON2 converts several nonconvex optimizers into approximate local-minimum methods using gradient computations alone.

paragraphs: This paper develops neural architectures that account for substitutions, insertions, and deletions in biological sequences. These edit operations are central to the evolution of proteins and DNA, so handling them is a natural concern for sequence models. In particular, insertions and deletions change how positions in different sequences correspond.

The authors propose two architectural approaches. One uses differentiable versions of the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm to build edit-invariant networks. The other uses deep convolutional networks with concatenations. Their analysis shows that CNNs can recognize star-free regular expressions, and that greater depth allows recognition of more complex expressions, including patterns involving inserted or deleted characters.

Experiments on protein secondary structure prediction suggest that insertion and deletion handling matters for this task. The reported test accuracy on CB513 is 71.5%, exceeding the then-best non-ensemble result by 1.2 percentage points. Together, the analysis and experiments connect sequence-edit structure to neural representation capacity and predictive performance, with the experimental evidence supporting the importance of these operations in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2018-neural-edit-operations-for-.tldr: Neural architectures that handle biological sequence edits improve protein secondary structure prediction in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Nonlocal neural networks allow features to interact across long distances in feature space. This paper investigates the behavior of those interactions, focusing on their diffusion and damping effects. The motivation is to understand the dynamics of nonlocal operations that have already proved useful in several computer vision tasks.

The authors analyze the spectra of weight matrices from trained networks and use that study to propose a revised nonlocal block. The new block learns nonlocal interactions while having stable dynamics. This stability allows deeper nonlocal structures, linking the mathematical behavior of an individual block to how extensively such blocks can be composed within a network.

The paper also interprets the proposed architecture through the broader framework of nonlocal modeling. It connects the network to nonlocal diffusion processes and Markov jump processes. These connections give a mathematical perspective on how distant features exchange information and how that interaction evolves. The contribution combines analysis of trained networks with an architectural formulation whose stated stability supports greater nonlocal depth.
neurips-2018-nonlocal-neural-networks-no.tldr: Analysis of nonlocal network dynamics leads to a stable block formulation that supports deeper nonlocal architectures.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately an unknown Markov chain can be learned from a single sequence of observations. It distinguishes two goals: predicting the next observation’s conditional distribution and estimating the whole transition matrix. Both are evaluated through minimax risk, which asks about expected loss under the most difficult chain in the considered class.

For next-step prediction measured by KL divergence, the authors establish lower and upper risk bounds of order k log log n/n and k² log log n/n. Here k is the number of states and n is the sequence length. The bounds therefore locate the minimax prediction risk within a factor linear in the number of states.

Transition-matrix estimation behaves differently. If transition probabilities may be arbitrarily small, the authors obtain only trivial uniform upper bounds on risk. They therefore impose a positive lower bound on those probabilities and resolve the estimation problem for essentially all sufficiently smooth f-divergences. The covered measures include KL, L2, chi-squared, Hellinger, and alpha divergences, showing why the transition-probability assumption matters.
neurips-2018-on-learning-markov-chains-8.tldr: The paper bounds Markov-chain prediction risk and characterizes transition estimation when probabilities are bounded away from zero.

paragraphs: This paper considers maximizing a submodular function when only an approximate version of it is available. Submodular structure makes many selection problems amenable to optimization, but guarantees based on exact structure can cease to hold when the observed objective is only approximate. The central question is how to recover meaningful guarantees from an imperfect surrogate.

The authors introduce a technique called sampled mean approximation. It supports maximization from approximate surrogates under two types of feasibility rules: a cardinality constraint, which limits selection size, and an intersection of matroid constraints. This places approximation in the objective alongside restrictions on which subsets may be selected.

The results include tight guarantees for the cardinality-constrained problem and a 1/(1+P) approximation guarantee when feasibility is defined by the intersection of P matroids. The latter explicitly relates the guarantee to the number of matroid constraints. The contribution is a principled way to optimize using approximate access to a submodular objective while retaining guarantees for these stated constraint families.
neurips-2018-optimization-for-approximat.tldr: Sampled mean approximation provides optimization guarantees when a submodular objective is accessible only through an approximate surrogate.

paragraphs: This paper helps image captioning models learn visual concepts beyond those covered by paired images and complete sentences. Labeled images and object detection datasets contain useful concept information, but usually do not provide full captions. The authors treat image labels and object classes as partial descriptions that can still supervise a captioning model.

They formulate the task as learning from partially specified sequences and represent those sequences using finite state automata. A new training algorithm allows sequence models, including recurrent neural networks, to use this form of supervision. It can be applied to an existing captioning model, expanding usable training data without requiring a specialized architecture for the alternative annotations.

On the COCO novel-object captioning task, the approach achieves the reported state of the art. The authors also teach a captioning model new concepts using Open Images while maintaining competitive COCO evaluation scores. These findings show that incomplete descriptive supervision can expand a model’s visual vocabulary while preserving competitive performance on the established captioning evaluation.
neurips-2018-partially-supervised-image-.tldr: Training on partially specified captions lets existing captioning models learn new visual concepts from labels and detection datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions with binary rewards, where each available action has contextual features. The learner must discover which actions work well while also choosing actions likely to pay off. The objective is low regret: limiting the reward lost through imperfect choices while learning from experience.

The proposed method, PG-TS, improves Thompson sampling through fast Bayesian inference using Polya-Gamma augmentation variables. An efficient Gibbs sampler approximates an integral in logistic contextual bandits that cannot be solved analytically. The approach explicitly estimates the posterior distribution of the context-feature covariance, making that uncertainty structure part of the decision process.

On simulated and real data, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, efficient exploration, and rapid convergence toward low-regret solutions. They attribute substantial empirical gains over approximate approaches to explicit covariance-posterior estimation. The contribution is both an inference procedure and evidence that Polya-Gamma augmentation is useful for bandit decisions. Its reported advantage comes from the evaluated settings, where improved uncertainty estimation supports the balance between exploration and reward-seeking.
neurips-2018-pg-ts-improved-thompson-sam.tldr: PG-TS uses Polya-Gamma Bayesian inference to improve exploration and reduce regret in logistic contextual bandit experiments.

paragraphs: This paper addresses learning problems where the true performance measure is difficult to optimize and a suitable surrogate objective is hard to choose. Instead of fixing that surrogate in advance, the learner repeatedly adapts its objective using preference feedback from an oracle. The learning loop therefore adjusts what it optimizes as well as the predictor itself.

When the objective admits a linear parameterization, the authors show that objective adaptation can be handled through a dueling bandit formulation. They propose DL²M, a sampling-based algorithm for learning the optimal parameter, with strong theoretical guarantees and efficient empirical performance. The linear parameterization is the stated condition enabling this connection.

Changing the objective could otherwise require training a hypothesis anew each time. To avoid that repeated cost, the authors introduce a boosting-based procedure that adapts a previously learned element hypothesis to the current objective. They apply the combined approach to multi-label learning and report strong performance across multiple measures. The work links preference-guided objective selection with efficient reuse of learned predictors.
neurips-2018-preference-based-adaptation.tldr: Preference feedback guides adaptation of linearly parameterized learning objectives, while boosting reuses existing predictors after objective changes.

paragraphs: Reinforced Continual Learning addresses the challenge of learning tasks one after another while retaining knowledge from earlier tasks. A model must fit each new task, but updates can interfere with what it previously learned. The paper focuses on both sides of that problem: accommodating new knowledge and reducing catastrophic forgetting.

The proposed approach uses reinforcement learning strategies to search for a suitable neural architecture for each incoming task. Architecture selection becomes part of the continual-learning process, allowing the system to seek a structure suited to the task currently being learned. The method is presented as a way to support new-task performance while preserving previously acquired capabilities.

Experiments use sequential classification tasks built from variants of MNIST and CIFAR-100. In those evaluations, the approach outperforms existing continual-learning alternatives for deep networks and shows good performance in preventing forgetting while fitting new tasks. These results support reinforcement-guided architecture search as a useful mechanism for continual learning, with the stated evidence coming from the tested task sequences.
neurips-2018-reinforced-continual-learni.tldr: Reinforcement-guided architecture search improves new-task learning and reduces forgetting in sequential classification experiments.

paragraphs: SLANG addresses the computational difficulty of estimating uncertainty in large neural networks. Even approximating the posterior with a Gaussian can be expensive. Common diagonal covariance approximations simplify that calculation, but the authors identify their poor uncertainty estimates as a reason to retain more structure without paying the cost of a full covariance representation.

The method uses stochastic, low-rank, approximate natural gradients for variational inference. It estimates a diagonal-plus-low-rank structure using only back-propagated gradients of the network log-likelihood. The low-rank component adds structure beyond a diagonal approximation. The procedure requires strictly fewer gradient computations than methods that differentiate the complete variational objective.

Evaluations on standard benchmarks find faster and more accurate uncertainty estimation than mean-field methods, with performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches. These results support the proposed compromise between computational cost and a richer approximation to uncertainty. The contribution is an inference method that obtains its structured approximation from familiar network gradients while improving the reported uncertainty estimates over simpler approximations.
neurips-2018-slang-fast-structured-covar.tldr: SLANG uses a diagonal-plus-low-rank approximation to estimate neural-network uncertainty efficiently from likelihood gradients.

paragraphs: This paper seeks common hidden structure in the spike trains of neural populations while allowing repeated trials to unfold differently. Variation can affect both the trajectory of the underlying computation and how quickly it progresses. Separating those effects is central to identifying shared activity without confusing timing changes with changes in the trajectory itself.

The approach extends Gaussian Process Factor Analysis using linearly combined shared latent Gaussian processes. A continuous-time point-process likelihood handles unbinned spike trains, and a sparse variational approximation provides scalability. The model separates condition-dependent effects from trial-specific trajectory variation. A nested Gaussian process formulation then represents differences in the rate of progression along a trajectory.

On synthetic data, the method recovers latent trajectories. Applied to motor cortical recordings, it accurately identifies trial-to-trial timing of movement-related parameters without supervision. These findings show that modeling trajectory variation and temporal progression together can reveal shared neural structure and movement-related timing directly from the observed population activity.
neurips-2018-temporal-alignment-and-late.tldr: A scalable Gaussian process model separates neural trajectory variation from timing variation in unbinned population spike trains.

paragraphs: This paper interprets meta-reinforcement learning as learning how to quickly obtain a useful sampling distribution in a new environment. Under this view, adaptation involves learning how to gather experience that supports effective behavior. The distribution of sampled experience becomes a central part of the learning problem rather than merely the source of training observations.

That interpretation leads to two algorithms, E-MAML and E-RL². The paper emphasizes correctly differentiating through sampling distributions in meta-reinforcement learning. This matters to the proposed perspective because learning how to adapt must account for how the learner’s behavior determines the experience it collects in a new environment.

The authors introduce Krazy World, a difficult high-dimensional gridworld designed to expose the importance of that sampling treatment. They also evaluate the algorithms on maze environments. Both E-MAML and E-RL² perform better than the baseline algorithms on the two tasks. The findings support the paper’s sampling-centered account of adaptation in these evaluations and motivate explicitly considering experience collection when designing meta-reinforcement learning methods.
neurips-2018-the-importance-of-sampling-.tldr: Treating adaptation as learning a useful sampling distribution produces two meta-RL algorithms that improve performance on gridworld and maze tasks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why unfolding an iterative sparse-recovery algorithm into a neural network can accelerate recovery. It focuses on unfolded ISTA, connecting its learned network structure to convergence toward the true sparse signal. The aim is to turn empirical success into mathematical guidance for choosing weights and thresholds.

The authors identify a weight structure necessary for asymptotic convergence to the true signal. With that structure, unfolded ISTA can achieve linear convergence, improving on the general sublinear convergence of ISTA and FISTA. The distinction matters: the structural condition is necessary for the stated asymptotic goal, while linear convergence is a capability established for the structured approach.

They further introduce thresholding that performs support selection, helping identify which signal entries belong in the sparse solution. This addition is easy to implement and improves convergence rates both theoretically and empirically. Simulations for sparse vector recovery and a compressive-sensing experiment on real images support the analysis and demonstrate the practical value of the proposed weights and thresholds.
neurips-2018-theoretical-linear-converge.tldr: Structured weights and support-selecting thresholds give unfolded ISTA theoretical and empirical improvements in sparse-recovery convergence.

paragraphs: STRSAGA is designed to maintain a machine-learning model as new training examples arrive over time. The goal is to update the model quickly while keeping its quality close to what could be achieved with advance access to the data. This makes ongoing model quality, rather than only eventual training performance, central to the problem.

The authors analyze STRSAGA competitively against an offline algorithm that receives the entire dataset beforehand. They compare the suboptimality of the maintained model and study risk competitiveness under different arrival patterns. This comparison makes the informational disadvantage of streaming explicit: the online method must act before seeing the full collection of examples.

The theoretical and experimental results show risk comparable to offline algorithms across a variety of input arrival patterns. Experiments also find significantly better performance than streaming methods including SGD and SSVRG. Together, these findings support STRSAGA as an efficient way to keep a model updated while retaining competitive quality under the arrival patterns considered in the study.
neurips-2018-variance-reduced-stochastic.tldr: STRSAGA updates models on arriving data while achieving risk comparable to offline methods across varied arrival patterns.
